findings.sentence: Students screening positive for two or more mental disorders had lower median vigorous physical activity than those screening negative (12.0 vs 16.3 MET-h/week; p<0.01) and slightly higher sedentary time (5.3 vs 5.0 h/day; p<0.01), while differences in moderate, walking, and total physical activity were not statistically significant.

Students screening positive for two or more mental disorders had lower median vigorous physical activity than those screening negative (12.0 vs 16.3 MET-h/week; p<0.01) and slightly higher sedentary time (5.3 vs 5.0 h/day; p<0.01), while differences in moderate, walking, and total physical activity were not statistically significant.

Students screening positive for a mood disorder had lower median vigorous, moderate, and total physical activity (8.3 vs 16.0, 4.5 vs 6.0, and 39.6 vs 44.8 MET-h/week, respectively) and higher sedentary time (5.5 vs 5.1 h/day; all p≤0.01), whereas walking levels were similar.

A comparable pattern was observed for anxiety disorders, with lower vigorous, moderate, and total physical activity (8.3 vs 16.3, 4.1 vs 6.4, and 38.4 vs 46.7 MET-h/week) and higher sedentary time (5.6 vs 5.0 h/day; all p<0.01), but no difference in walking.

Students reporting suicidal ideation had lower vigorous, moderate, and total physical activity (9.3 vs 16.0, 4.3 vs 6.0, and 39.2 vs 45.3 MET-h/week) and higher sedentary time (5.5 vs 5.1 h/day; all p<0.01), while walking levels did not differ.

Finally, students screening positive for an eating disorder had higher median walking and total physical activity than those screening negative (13.0 vs 11.8 MET-h/week, p<0.01; and 45.3 vs 42.0 MET-h/week, p=0.01), with no significant differences in vigorous or moderate activity or sedentary time.

findings.sentence: The adaptive staircase procedure effectively controlled task difficulty by adjusting target opacity levels, resulting in different opacity thresholds between valid and invalid trials (t(14) = 2.94, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.76).

Discrimination accuracy and visibility ratings did not differ between valid and invalid cueing trials and remained stable across task blocks (all p > 0.60; Greenhouse-Geisser correction applied where appropriate).
Although task performance was stable, reaction times were significantly faster on valid compared to invalid trials (634 ± 137 vs. 725 ± 159 ms; t(14) = 3.44, p < 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.89; Figure 2A).

Although cueing did not affect overall visibility, participants became more conservative at invalid cue trials (i.e. response bias; t(14) = 2.38, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.62; Figure 2B), and they also displayed a reduced metacognitive efficiency (t(14) = 1.89, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.49; Figure 2C).

Although cueing did not affect overall visibility, participants became more conservative at invalid cue trials (i.e. response bias; t(14) = 2.38, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.62; Figure 2B), and they also displayed a reduced metacognitive efficiency (t(14) = 1.89, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.49; Figure 2C).

As in Experiment 1, discrimination accuracy, visibility ratings and perceptual sensitivity did not differ with cue validity, stimulation site, or task block (all p > 0.05; Greenhouse-Geisser corrections applied where appropriate).

Unlike in Experiment 1, opacity levels and response bias did not differ between cue conditions or stimulation sites (all p > 0.10), indicating comparable task difficulty and familiarization with the task.
Reaction times showed a main effect of cue validity (F(1,15) = 6.72, p < 0.05, η² p = 0.58), but not stimulation site (p = 0.89).
Interestingly, valid cues speed responses following S1-cTBS (V = 6, p < 0.05, rrb = 1), whereas this cueing effect was absent after DLPFC-cTBS (p = 0.07; Figure 3A).

Also consistent with Experiment 1, invalid cues reduced metacognitive efficiency following S1-cTBS (V = 6, p < 0.05, rrb = 0.81), whereas this effect disappeared after DLPFC-cTBS (p = 0.42; Figure 3B).
Nonparametric metacognitive sensitivity (A′) likewise decreased for invalid cues following S1-cTBS (V = 3, p < 0.05, rrb = 0.77), but not after DLPFC-cTBS (p = 0.53).

Trial-by-trial analyses showed no significant effects following S1-cTBS (all p > 0.40), whereas following DLPFC-cTBS, two consecutive invalid-cue trials significantly reduced metacognitive efficiency (V = 27, p < 0.05, rrb = 0.93; Figure 4A).

Trial-by-trial analyses showed no significant effects following S1-cTBS (all p > 0.40), whereas following DLPFC-cTBS, two consecutive invalid-cue trials significantly reduced metacognitive efficiency (V = 27, p < 0.05, rrb = 0.93; Figure 4A).
Finally, the Gratton effect on reaction time was significantly smaller following DLPFC-cTBS than following S1-cTBS (V = 21, p < 0.05, rrb = 0.90; Figure 4B).
